rationale: A woman of the land of Canaan, outside Israel, speaks to Israelites about Israel's God and asks for her family to be spared. Rahab says "the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below" and asks the spies to "spare the lives of my father and mother" (Joshua 2:11, 2:13, BSB); Joshua 6:25 records that she was spared "with her father's household." The Canaanite woman calls Jesus "Lord, Son of David" and asks for her daughter (Matthew 15:22). Matthew itself has already named Rahab, in the genealogy (1:5). Amy-Jill Levine (Currents in Theology and Mission, 2007) writes that Matthew's "Canaanite" "reminds readers of Canaanite women in the genealogy, Tamar and Rahab, who proved more faithful than the men with whom they are associated." Graded motif, not allusion, because Matthew 15 shares no wording with Joshua 2 and does not name Rahab; and plausible, not strong, because only Matthew's one word "Canaanite" points back. Joshua 2 calls Rahab a resident of Jericho and does not use the word "Canaanite" of her, and Genesis 38 does not state Tamar's people (it calls Shua, Judah's father-in-law, a Canaanite, 38:2). So the shared category is Levine's reading of Matthew, which this row reports.
